A revised rule set and expansion of the original stealth game created by Jonathan Gilmour

Revision by Matt Mason

POCKET DUNGEON 2.0 is a revision of the original deluxe-version solitaire dungeon crawl in which you create a hero and explore a dungeon that is generated as you play. The objective is to clear the dungeon of its monster inhabitants, locate the boss monster, and defeat it.

SET UP

To play DUN-GEN, you will need:

• 1x printed Adventure Sheet

• 1x pencil and eraser

• 1x six-sided die (d6)

• 1x eight-sided die (d8)

The following are optional references that will save the player much rule book page-flipping:

• 1x printed Profession Reference Sheet

• 1x printed Treasure Reference Sheet

• 1x printed Spell Book Sheet

Gather the Adventure Sheet and your pencil. In the bottom-center square of the map grid on the Adventure Sheet, draw a horizontal wall with a door. This is the entrance to the dungeon your hero will be exploring.

Next, select the monsters that will inhabit the dungeon you are about to explore. For your first adventure, select any one of the monster packages from the Tier 1 section of the Monster Manual at the end of this rule book. Copy the monsters and their stats from this package into the Monsters Table of the Adventure Sheet. Record the 1st monster in the rooms 1-9 row, the 2nd monster in the rooms 10- 19 row, the 3rd monster in the rooms 20-29 row, and the 4th (Boss) monster in the room 30 row.

Now, let’s create your hero…

maximum Action Points (Max AP) = 2 x Willpower

The first step in creating your hero is to name them. Record this name in the Hero box of the Adventure Sheet.

The next step in creating your hero is to select a race for them.

Race: Your choice of race will impose modifiers on the hero’s attributes that you generate later in the process of creating your hero.

Human (the base race) No modifications to attributes

Elf (the noble forestral race) +1 to Agility or Willpower, -3 to Max HP

Half Elf (the versatile race) +1 additional Fudge Point per 10 monsters defeated, -3 to Max HP

Dwarf (the stalwart race) +3 to Max HP, -1 to Agility

Gnome (the tinkering race) +1 Bonus Rating at start of every dungeon, +1 to Agility or Willpower, -3 to Max HP, -1 to Strength

Halfling (the nimble race) +1 to Agility, -1 to Strength

Half Orc (the brutish race) +1 to Strength, +3 to Max HP, -2 to Willpower

Record your hero’s race in the Hero box at the top of the Adventure Sheet. Now that you have selected a race, the next step is to assign your hero’s attributes.

Assigning attributes The player distributes 9 points between Strength, Agility and Willpower; with no more than 5 points assigned to any 1 attribute. The attributes are then adjusted according to any modifiers from the race selected for the hero. Points must be assigned to cancel any negative modifiers. A hero may not start the game with a negative value for an attribute.

Example: We decide to create a Dwarf hero. As a Dwarf, this hero will suffer a -1 adjustment to Agility. The player may assign no more than 5 points to any one attribute. We could assign 5 points to Strength resulting in a Strength attribute of 5. We must also assign at least 1 point to Agility to make sure we cancel out the -1 adjustment. The remaining 3 points can be distributed between Agility and Willpower.

Alternatively, we could assign the 5 points maximum to Agility, and wind up with an Agility attribute of 4 (after adjustment). The remaining 4 points can be distributed between Strength and Willpower.

Record the hero’s final adjusted Strength, Agility, and Willpower attributes on the Adventure Sheet. Also record the calculated Movement and maximum Action Points (Max AP) values. Now, it is time to select a profession for your hero.

Pocket Dungeon is what I have come to call a "stealth-game" or “ninja-game”. What that is, is a game that can be played out in the open without people knowing you are playing a game. Pocket Dungeon at its core is a Dungeon generator (the DunGen system) and slimmed down Dungeon crawler. The cool part about this, is this game also serves as a tutorial on how to stealth-game using items you will find (or would not look out of place) on your office or school desk. Pocket Dungeon is completely free to print and play, but if you enjoy the game and would like donation information, it can be found in the FAQ at the end.

The goal in Pocket Dungeon is very simple: Enter a dungeon, kill lots of stuff, get phat lewt, bring death to the Boss and try to avoid Death's clammy grip. And don't get caught by your boss or co- workers while doing it\!

Setup and the road less traveled.

Now my friend let me show you the way of lost productivity. It’s time to make our stealth gaming supplies. You may skip this section if you plan on using dice along with the Deluxe version. If you go that route, every time you see \*flip\* in the manual, pretend it says \*roll\*.

Here is what you will need:

1 copy of Pocket Dungeon printed off, and folded using the folding guide on (http://www.pocketmod.com/howto/ ) 1 small stack of post-it style notes. The really little ones if you can find them for added stealth.. Big ones should work too though. 1 Pencil. I like mechanical you can use old fashion, let your conscience be your guide on this one. 1 Slacker attitude and a real commitment to avoiding work.

Now, do the following steps in order:

1 - Print off the Pocket Dungeon sheet, and fold it up really nice. Spend a few minutes on this. You really didn't need to get that report done any time soon, did you? Folded up proper? It should look like a ToDo list on the front, followed by the (patent-pending) DunGen page, and then a page of graph paper, and then another DunGen chart and associated graph. The two pages before the last are extra charts and character generation information. Each Pocket Dungeon sheet will contain enough space for two Dungeons. 2 - Take your stack of post-it style notes. Flip to the very last one. Write 1 in the bottom right hand corner. Flip to the next sheet. Write a 2. Repeat this process until you reach six. Are you there yet? good. Now flip to the next sheet, and start over at 1. Repeat 1-6 until you are about 3/4ths of the way through the stack. 3 - Now go back to the bottom note and on the bottom left start at 1 and then progress to 8. All the way up the stack. Take your time. This will become your stealth dice. If you are REALLY avoiding work, you can also throw a 1-20 in the middle and play some DnD at your desk. 4 - Take the stack of post-it style notes. Press them firmly against the desk. Put your thumb on the bottom right hand corner. Now riffle through the sheets and stop somewhere. See what we just did? All the random joy of a d6 with none of the clanky clank. The other corner is a d8. These are the only two dice you will need for Pocket Dungeon. If you ever need a d4, just use 1-4 on the d8 side, and then again 5-8. Sneaky eh?

The Game as she is played.

Now it is time for me to introduce you to the patent pending DunGen system.

Looks like a just a random bunch of letters and numbers huh? I like to call this game camouflage. But you are a smart gamer; you should be able to make sense out of this after I detail how to use it. Mastering this system should give you a sense of accomplishment, hopefully more so then the work you are avoiding doing by playing games. First, before I get into what the Letters mean, let’s look at how to read the numbers, shall we?

When you see something like this: 1-3 – X 4-5 – Y 6 – Z

Read it like this. On a roll of 1 to 3, do X. On a 4 or 5, do Y. And If I roll a 6, then I will do Z. Simple enough.

These letters, they must mean something\!\!

• S - Size of the room that you are entering. This is how many squares it should take up. But what shape you ask? I don't care. This is part of the fun of Pocket Dungeon, using the random rolls to make your dungeon. Roll a 3, make a room that’s 4 squares. It can be a hallway, a square room, or some other crazy shape. The only rule while drawing rooms, is that it cannot result in there being squares without rooms trapped somewhere on the map.

• \#D - Number of added doors. Obviously the room already has one door, you walked through it, right? Since you are entering a room for the first time, this is how many other exits you see. Where do you put them? Don't put it right next to the one you came in from, unless it would lead to a different room then the one you just came out of. Still can't figure it out, then use the handy Dd chart.

• L - Door/Treasure lockedness (yeah, I know it’s not a real word). Is the door, locked, unlocked, or some other mystical quantum state? Only this chart can tell. blocks.text:
Good question. They're the same app, but option 3 adds **persistence and the between-dungeons meta-game**. Here's the breakdown:

**Option 1 (Full play assistant)** handles one adventure, start to finish:
- Create a hero, generate rooms, fight, loot, track HP/AP/map
- Great for sitting down and playing through a single dungeon
- When you close the app or finish the dungeon, the session is basically done. You'd re-create your hero next time.

**Option 3 (Full + dungeon persistence)** is option 1 **plus** the parts of the rulebook that span *across* sessions and dungeons:

1. **Save & resume mid-dungeon** — close the app at room 14, come back tomorrow, pick up exactly where you left off (hero HP, the map you've drawn, monsters remaining, inventory).

2. **A persistent hero roster** — your heroes are saved. "Thornwick the Dwarf Cleric, Tier 3, 47 gold" is still there next week.

3. **The "Continuing the Adventure" meta-game** — the rulebook has a whole between-dungeons loop that option 1 ignores:
   - **Dungeon tiers**: finish a Tier 1 dungeon → your hero advances to Tier 2 (tougher monster packages)
   - **Selling equipment** for gold (the price chart: weapons = R+D+H, armor = 3×A, etc.)
   - **Upgrading items** by spending gold and applying Bonus Rating (e.g. boost a found sword from D2 H0 → D3 H1)
   - **Permanent progression**: Fudge Points → permanent stat boosts, Bonus Rating accumulating as you explore

So the real question is: **do you want this to remember a long-running hero who grows over many dungeons, or is it more of a "play a dungeon when I feel like it" tool where re-rolling a fresh hero is fine?**

The tradeoff: option 3 is the truest to how Pocket Dungeon is actually designed to be played long-term, but it's a meaningfully bigger build (save files, hero management UI, the sell/upgrade economy screens). Option 1 gets you playing the core loop sooner.

Want me to re-pose the scope question, or does this clear it up enough to pick?

# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.10"
# dependencies = [

#   "pyobjc-framework-WebKit",

"""
Pocket Dungeon desktop shell — runs the Flask server in-process and renders it
in a native macOS WKWebView window (via pywebview). Falls back to the default
browser if pywebview is unavailable.

Run directly with uv (handles deps):  uv run --script desktop.py
"""
import os
import sys
import threading
import time
import urllib.request
import webbrowser

import app as pd

URL = f"http://127.0.0.1:{pd.PORT}/"

# Tee logs to a file — the .app launches detached, so stdout goes nowhere.
try:
    _logf = open(os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), "desktop.log"), "a", buffering=1)
    sys.stdout = sys.stderr = _logf
except Exception:
    pass


def _server_up():
    try:
        urllib.request.urlopen(URL + "api/health", timeout=1)
        return True
    except Exception:
        return False


def main():
    if _server_up():
        print("Pocket Dungeon is already running.")
        webbrowser.open(URL)
        return

    pd.start_background()  # init the SQLite DB
    threading.Thread(
        target=lambda: pd.app.run(host="127.0.0.1", port=pd.PORT,
                                  debug=False, threaded=True, use_reloader=False),
        daemon=True,
    ).start()
    for _ in range(160):  # wait up to ~40s for the server
        if _server_up():
            break
        time.sleep(0.25)

    try:
        import webview
        webview.create_window("Pocket Dungeon", URL, width=1240, height=860, min_size=(900, 640))
        webview.start()  # blocks on the native GUI loop until the window closes
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"pywebview unavailable ({e}); opening in browser.")
        webbrowser.open(URL)
        while True:  # keep the server alive
            time.sleep(3600)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# Pocket Dungeon

A local web app for running **Pocket Dungeon 2.0** digitally — the solo
dungeon-crawl system created by Jonathan Gilmour, revised/expanded by Matt
Mason. It automates the tedious bits (dice, the DUN-GEN room generator, combat
math, treasure tables, progression) while leaving the map and tactical
positioning to you, just like the paper game.

This is an unofficial play aid for personal use. All rules content belongs to
its creators; source PDFs live in Google Drive under
`3.) Reference/Games/Pocket Dungeon`.

## What it does

- **Hero roster** — create heroes (race + attributes + profession), saved in a
  local SQLite DB. Resume mid-dungeon or carry a hero across many dungeons.
- **Hero creation** — distribute 9 attribute points (max 5 each), auto-applies
  race modifiers, auto-derives Movement / Max AP, and rolls Max HP
  (`profession base + best of 2d6 + race mod`).
- **DUN-GEN** — one click rolls room size, doors, locks & traps, monster count
  (with the right monster type for the room depth), and treasure / Special
  Rooms. Boss waits in room 30.
- **Combat tracker** — pick a monster, attack with your equipped weapon or a
  memorized combat spell; the app rolls `d6 + attack skill + Hit` vs Defense and
  applies damage. "Monsters Attack" rolls each monster's attack and applies
  damage net of your Armor (mitigated once per round, per the rules).
- **Treasure** — loot checks and chests roll the full Treasure Type → item
  chain and drop the result into your inventory, with your current Bonus Rating
  auto-applied to new gear.
- **Progression** — Bonus Rating (+1 / 5 rooms), Fudge Points (+1 / 5 kills,
  +half-elf bonus), permanent stat/HP boosts, tier advancement, and selling
  equipment between dungeons.
- **Paintable grid map** — sketch the dungeon as you explore (floor / doors /
  hero / monsters / chests / room numbers). Entrance pre-marked.
- **Rulebook tab** — the full Monster Manual (Tiers 1–3), weapons, armor,
  spells, potions/scrolls/magic items, professions & abilities, races, and the
  DUN-GEN / progression tables, all searchable in-app.
- **Dice dock** — floating d6 / d8 / d20 roller and a running combat log.

## Running it

```bash
# from this directory
uv run --script desktop.py        # native window (installs deps on first run)
```

or with the bundled venv (browser):

```bash
./.venv/bin/python app.py         # then open http://127.0.0.1:5009/
```

A **Pocket Dungeon.app** launcher is installed in `~/Desktop/Apps/` — double
click it to start the server and open the native window.

## Files

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `app.py` | Flask server: serves the SPA + SQLite hero roster (CRUD + autosave) on port **5009** |
| `static/gamedata.js` | All Pocket Dungeon 2.0 content as structured data |
| `static/app.js` | The single-page game client (state, combat, DUN-GEN, UI) |
| `static/style.css` | Dark dungeon theme |
| `templates/index.html` | App shell |
| `desktop.py` | pywebview launcher (PEP 723 inline deps, runs via `uv`) |
| `pocket_dungeon.db` | Local save data (gitignored) |

State autosaves to the DB on every change, so you can close and resume any time.

## Notes on faithfulness

The app automates resolvable mechanics and shows the rules text for everything
it doesn't fully simulate. A few deliberately manual areas (the game is still
yours to adjudicate):

- **Map & positioning / line-of-sight / range** — you paint the map and decide
  who's in range; the attack buttons trust your targeting.
- **Multi-attack bosses** (Murke, Magus, Tyrranus, etc.) use a single
  representative attack line in the tracker; their full attack profile is shown
  in the monster's special text to apply by hand.
- **Bonus Rating on found gear** defaults to damage (weapons) / armor value
  (armor); the rules let you split it across D/H or add aspects — adjust as you
  like.
- **Profession abilities, scrolls, and non-combat spells** are listed for
  reference; spend AP and apply effects via the HP/AP steppers.

A faithful digital play-aid for the **Pocket Dungeon 2.0** solo dungeon-crawl, built from the rulebook in your Drive. It automates the tedious paper bits and leaves the creative bits (map, positioning) to you:

- **Treasure + progression** — loot checks/chests roll the full item chain with Bonus Rating auto-applied; Fudge Points, permanent boosts, tier advancement, and selling between dungeons.

1. Select the **Door 🚪** tool.

## Designating walls
1. Pick the **Wall ▬** tool (new, next to Floor in the palette).

3. Click a wall again to **remove** it.

## How walls, doors, and floors fit together
This now matches the paper game's model exactly:
- **Floor** tool fills the room's *squares*.
- **Wall ▬** tool draws the room outline on the *segments* around those squares.
- **Door 🚪** tool places an opening *in* a wall (and cycles unlocked → 🔒 locked → ⚠ trapped → off).

The tools cooperate sensibly: using the **Door** tool on a wall segment turns it into a door (an opening); using the **Wall** tool on a door turns it back into solid wall; **Erase** clears either. The entrance stays a door through all of it.

The **legend** under the map now shows: wall · door · 🔒 locked · ⚠ trapped, and the hint text updates per tool to explain segment-clicking.

Live on next launch/refresh. So a typical room now: paint the floor squares → outline them with walls → drop doors on the segments where the checklist says (with the right lock/trap state) → place monsters/chests/hero in the squares.
